system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2170-05-21 21:21:00 to 2170-05-22 16:52:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a 58-year-old male with a history of acute myeloid leukemia s/p allogeneic cord transplant and chronic graft-versus-host disease, was admitted for nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea lasting five days. He was found to be dehydrated with orthostatic hypotension and acute kidney injury, with creatinine rising from a baseline of 1.8 to 3.0. IV hydration was initiated, and his renal function improved, returning to baseline by discharge. Stool testing was positive for norovirus, and flexible sigmoidoscopy with biopsy showed no evidence of graft-versus-host disease. Liver enzymes remained elevated throughout admission, prompting consultation with the liver team and plans for close outpatient monitoring; allopurinol was discontinued, and Bactrim was held due to transaminitis. The patient's gastrointestinal symptoms resolved, and he was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to follow up on liver function and restart medications as appropriate.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS:  Perirectal abscess.

INVASIVE PROCEDURES ON THIS ADMISSION:  Examination under

CHIEF COMPLAINT:  Perianal pain over several days.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:  Mr. ___ is a ___
gentleman with a recent 9-day admission to the Oncology
service with nausea, vomiting, diarrhea.  He had a flexible
sigmoidoscopy on that admission and he was subsequently
discharged on ___.  He had worsening perianal pain since
discharge and presented to the emergency room with perianal
pain and concern for a perirectal abscess.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:  AML with bone marrow transplant
complicated by GVHD, stage III chronic kidney disease,
hepatic insufficiency due to the hemochromatosis,
aspergillosis of the sinus and nares, sarcoid, hypertension,
reflux, chronic diarrhea hypercholesterolemia due to
peripheral neuropathy, diabetes, left lower lobe pneumonia
and basal cell cancers.

PAST SURGICAL HISTORY:  Basal cell cancer excision.

MEDICATIONS:  On admission were acyclovir, carvedilol,
citalopram, fluticasone, mycophenolate, nitroglycerin p.r.n.,
oxycodone, pantoprazole, prednisone, ascorbic acid, aspirin,
cholecalciferol, calcium carbonate, cyanocobalamin,
loratadine, procarbazine, Lomotil.

ALLERGIES:  Benadryl, AmBisone, Flomax and tacrolimus.

SOCIAL HISTORY: ___
FAMILY HISTORY:  Noncontributory.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:  On physical exam he was tachycardic
with left-sided perianal fullness and tenderness on digital
rectal exam.

SUMMARY OF HOSPITAL COURSE:  Mr. ___ was diagnosed

anesthesia with a large abscess drainage with cultures.  He

and he was deemed appropriate for discharge with follow-up in
the acute care surgery clinic and with his oncologist.

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS:  The same as preoperative medications

DISCHARGE STATUS:  The patient was discharged to home with

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you've been having increasing pain around your backside for a few days now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. It started a few days ago, but since I got home from the last hospital stay, it’s gotten much worse. It’s sharp and tender, especially when I sit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were just discharged from oncology for nausea and diarrhea, correct? Any fever or chills with this pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever that I’ve noticed, but my heart’s been racing. I thought it was just from being uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. On exam, I felt fullness on the left side near your rectum, and it’s quite tender. We’re concerned this could be a perirectal abscess — a pocket of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: An abscess? Like an infected cyst? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially with your medical history. Because you’ve had a transplant and are on immunosuppressants, infections can spread faster. We recommend draining it right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Draining it? Will I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s a minor procedure. You’ll go under anesthesia briefly, we’ll make a small incision to drain the pus, and place a small drain to keep it open so it can continue to drain over the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds reasonable. What happens after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start you on IV antibiotics for 24 hours, then switch to oral ones. A nurse will help you care for the drain at home, and you’ll follow up with the surgery clinic in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure went well. We drained a large abscess and placed a Malecot drain. Cultures were taken to check what kind of bacteria are causing the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Any idea what caused it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With your history of chronic diarrhea and immunosuppression, it’s not uncommon. The culture showed Group B Streptococcus and Bacteroides — both can be part of normal gut flora but can cause infection when they get into deeper tissues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the antibiotics clear it up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and because we caught it early and drained it, you should recover well. We’ll keep you on antibiotics and monitor the wound.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — you’re ready to go home today. The drain is functioning well, and you’re tolerating oral antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have a visiting nurse come by to help with wound irrigation and drain care. Keep taking the antibiotics, watch for fever or increased pain, and follow up with both surgery and your oncologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other medications — should I restart them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your previous medications should be continued, including prednisone and mycophenolate. We’ve added antibiotics to your list for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I’m glad we caught this in time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy, keep the area clean, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge papers are ready. A nurse will go over wound care instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll make sure to follow up with my oncologist too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your complex medical history means close follow-up is key. We’ll coordinate with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate that. I feel much better already.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a 58-year-old male with a history of acute myeloid leukemia in remission, chronic graft-versus-host disease, and multiple comorbidities, was admitted with worsening perianal pain following a recent hospitalization for gastrointestinal symptoms. He was found to have a perirectal abscess, confirmed on physical examination, and underwent examination under anesthesia with incision and drainage. A Malecot drain was placed for ongoing irrigation. Cultures from the abscess grew Group B Streptococcus and Bacteroides fragilis group. He received 24 hours of intravenous antibiotics followed by oral therapy. His condition stabilized quickly, and he was discharged home with visiting nursing support for wound care, instructions to continue all baseline medications plus antibiotics, and plans for follow-up with surgery and oncology. The hospital stay was brief and uncomplicated.
